advanced-industries.overview: Advanced industries covers engineering-heavy manufacturers: carmakers and their suppliers, aircraft and defense companies, and makers of industrial machinery and equipment. Products take years to design and depend on long, global supply chains, so these companies are shaped by how full their factories are, trade policy and the cost of materials like steel. A large share of their profit often comes from servicing and spare parts after the original sale.
advanced-industries.recap: Earnings season opened strongly. GM beat on North American trucks, raised its cash flow outlook and added a $20B buyback, while GE Aerospace (orders up 49%) and RTX ($340B backlog) both raised 2026 guidance on booming aftermarket and defense demand. 3M lifted its EPS outlook and signed an optical connectivity deal with Amazon. Watch for supply chain limits on deliveries and the hit from high fuel on airline customers. Tesla reports Wednesday.

consumer-retail.overview: Consumer and retail covers the companies that make and sell what people buy day to day. That includes stores and online retailers, makers of food, drinks and household products, farm and food businesses, and travel and hospitality companies like airlines and hotels. Consumer spending is about two-thirds of the US economy, so these businesses rise and fall with how confident people feel and how much money they have left after essentials.
consumer-retail.recap: Costs are the theme. Silgan and American Industrial Partners agreed to buy can maker Trivium for $3.4B, a cost-synergy play in packaging for food and pet food brands. S&P Global warned the Hormuz shock is raising fertilizer and diesel costs for farmers, with food prices likely to feel the full squeeze in 2027. Diesel near $6.30 is also adding freight surcharges. P&G reports Thursday.

energy-materials.overview: Energy and materials covers the companies that pull resources out of the ground and turn them into fuel, power and raw materials. That includes oil and gas producers, the pipelines, ships and terminals that move their output, refineries and chemical plants, electric utilities and renewable developers, and miners and steelmakers. These are capital-heavy businesses that live with commodity prices they don't control, so returns depend on keeping costs low and investing at the right point in the cycle.
energy-materials.recap: The sector is in a supply shock. Brent ended last week near $110 as Strait of Hormuz transits ran about 70% below pre-war levels, and IEA members coordinated a ~100M barrel stock release. Gas is just as tight: Asian LNG hit a near four-year high around $29/MMBtu and Europe enters winter with record-low 74% storage, while US gas sits near $3. In metals, tariff protection lifted Cleveland-Cliffs to its best quarter in three years. Key dates: EIA data Oct 21, OPEC+ meeting Nov 1.

financial-services.overview: Financial services is the business of managing, lending, investing and moving money. Banks take deposits and make loans, insurers collect premiums to cover risks, asset managers invest on behalf of savers and pension funds, and payments companies handle the flow of money between people and businesses. It is one of the most heavily regulated industries, so how much capital firms must hold and how well they control risk shapes how profitable they can be.
financial-services.recap: Enforcement is the theme. Bank of America took over $1.2B in penalties for anti-money-laundering failures, including a record $750M OCC fine, a week after American Express paid $350M for similar issues. Expect more compliance spending across the industry. Ameriprise fell about 3% Monday on a BofA downgrade.

healthcare.overview: Healthcare covers the companies that discover, make, pay for and deliver medical care. Drugmakers and biotech firms develop medicines, device makers build everything from surgical tools to heart implants, insurers pay for care, and hospitals and doctors provide it. In the US the system is large and complex, and prices are set through negotiation between manufacturers, insurers and the middlemen between them, so policy and regulation matter as much as science.
healthcare.recap: J&J beat profit expectations on ~8% drug sales growth, raised 2026 guidance and is leaning toward spinning off orthopedics, while warning that new drug acquisitions will weigh on 2027 earnings. The big-pharma pattern: focus on high-margin drugs, separate slower units, and buy pipeline to cover patent cliffs.

infrastructure-logistics.overview: Infrastructure and logistics covers the physical networks the rest of the economy runs on. That includes the trucking, rail, shipping and air freight companies that move goods, the developers and builders behind homes, offices and data centers, and the public sector that funds and regulates much of it. These businesses are sensitive to fuel costs and interest rates, because moving goods burns diesel and most buildings are paid for with borrowed money.
infrastructure-logistics.recap: Fuel and rates are the two pressures. Diesel near $6.30 a gallon has pushed freight surcharges across supply chains and left truckers on fixed contracts losing money. In real estate, homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest since 2012 with mortgages near 7.4% and 43% of builders cutting prices.

macro.overview: The macro picture covers the forces that move every industry at once: how fast economies are growing, how quickly prices are rising, where central banks set interest rates, and how goods and money flow between countries. When energy costs climb or borrowing gets more expensive, the effects show up in nearly every company's results, so this is the backdrop for reading the rest of the news.
macro.recap: Energy is driving the macro story. Oil above $100 and $6+ diesel lifted US core CPI to 2.6% in September, the 10-year yield is near 5.1%, and markets price some chance of a Fed hike at the Oct 27–28 meeting. China grew 4.5% in Q3 on a 36% jump in September exports while domestic demand stayed soft. Q3 GDP and September PCE inflation arrive next week.

tmt.overview: Tech, media and telecom covers the companies behind computing and communication: chipmakers, software and cloud providers, internet platforms like search and social media, entertainment and streaming companies, and the telecom networks that connect everything. Many of these businesses become more profitable as they grow, because serving one more customer costs very little, which is why a handful of very large companies dominate. Much of the sector's investment today is going into the data centers and chips that power AI.
tmt.recap: Tech had its worst week in months: the Nasdaq fell about 4.5% and chip stocks about 10% as investors questioned debt-funded AI buildouts, and CoreWeave dropped 25%+ before a Goldman upgrade. Private equity is buying software: Thoma Bravo's Proofpoint is acquiring Varonis for $6.3B, and Bumble is going private at $1.3B. Netflix (Tue) and Meta (Wed) earnings will test the AI spending story.

media-entertainment.operatingModel: Streamers collect monthly subscriptions and ad revenue and spend most of it on content, so profit depends on spreading a fixed content budget over more subscribers and higher prices. Operating margins for the leader run around 30%, while smaller rivals earn far less.
media-entertainment.overview: Media and entertainment companies make and distribute films, TV, music, games and news, and sell them through streaming subscriptions, advertising, cinemas and licensing. Content costs a lot to make but little to copy, so the winners are the services that spread those costs over the most viewers. Streaming has largely replaced cable, shifting money from bundles to monthly subscriptions and ads.

Video platforms such as YouTube and TikTok take viewing time

medtech.operatingModel: Makers sell the device or system once, then earn recurring revenue from disposable supplies, software and service contracts. Gross margins are high, around 60% to 70%, and spending on R&D and sales teams is the main cost.
medtech.overview: Medical technology companies make the devices, implants and equipment used in care, from surgical robots and heart valves to insulin pumps and imaging machines. They sell mainly to hospitals, which buy under tight budgets and care about clinical evidence. Once a device is installed and surgeons are trained on it, hospitals rarely switch, so a recurring stream of supplies and service follows the first sale.

payments-fintech.overview: Payments and fintech covers the networks, processors and apps that move money between people and businesses. power-utilities.operatingModel: Regulated utilities earn an allowed return on equity (typically around 9-10% in the US) on their rate base, so profit grows by investing more capital. Independent generators earn the market price of power minus fuel costs, which makes them more volatile.

In much of the US, utilities are regulated monopolies: a state commission sets their prices so they can recover costs and earn an allowed return on the grid and plants they build. Other markets separate generation, which competes on price, from transmission and distribution, which stay regulated.
